papers.title: Real-time detection of correlated quasiparticle tunneling events in a multi-qubit superconducting device
papers.abstract: Quasiparticle tunneling events are a source of decoherence and correlated errors in superconducting circuits. Understanding and ultimately mitigating these errors calls for real-time detection of quasiparticle tunneling events on individual devices. In this work, we simultaneously detect quasiparticle tunneling events in two co-housed, charge-sensitive transmons coupled to a common waveguide. We measure background quasiparticle tunneling rates at the single-hertz level, with temporal resolution of tens of microseconds. Using time-tagged coincidence analysis, we show that individual events are uncorrelated across devices, whereas burst episodes occur about once per minute and are largely correlated. These bursts have a characteristic lifetime of 7 ms and induce a thousand-fold increase in the quasiparticle tunneling rate across both devices. In addition, we identify a rarer subset of bursts which are accompanied by a shift in the offset charge, at approximately one event per hour. Our results establish a practical and extensible method to identify quasiparticle bursts in superconducting circuits, as well as their correlations and spatial structure, advancing routes to suppress correlated errors in superconducting quantum processors.

summary.summary: This work demonstrates real-time detection of quasiparticle tunneling events in two moderately charge-sensitive transmons ($E_J/E_C \approx 15$) coupled to a common waveguide, achieving single-hertz background resolution with 100 µs temporal resolution. The study reveals three distinct QP dynamics regimes: uncorrelated baseline switching ($\Gamma_\mathrm{slow}^{(1)} = 5.28$ s$^{-1}$, $\Gamma_\mathrm{slow}^{(2)} = 3.61$ s$^{-1}$), correlated bursts occurring ~1 min$^{-1}$ with thousand-fold rate enhancement ($\Gamma_\mathrm{fast} \sim 4000$ s$^{-1}$) and ~7 ms lifetime, and a rarer subset showing offset-charge shifts ($\sim1$–2 h$^{-1}$) consistent with ionizing events.
summary.motivation: QP tunneling bursts create correlated errors that violate the spatial and temporal independence assumptions of surface codes and other error-correction schemes, yet existing measurements average over ensemble timescales and cannot resolve individual burst events on chip.
summary.method: Two charge-sensitive transmons with maximum sensitivities of 11 MHz and 9 MHz per Cooper pair, separated by 1.5 mm, are continuously driven at their parity-dependent transition frequencies $\omega_\mathrm{01}^\pm$ and monitored via coherent microwave scattering through a common waveguide; parity switches are extracted from demodulated signals with discrimination fidelity $\mathcal{F} > 0.999$ using Gaussian mixture models, burst intervals identified via kernel density estimation with 20 ms kernel, and inter-device correlations quantified via intensity cross-correlation analysis.
summary.result: Of 197 bursts in detector 1 and 121 in detector 2, 92 are correlated ($R_{12}(0) > 1$ with peak at $\tau = 0$); uncorrelated background shows $R_{12}(\tau) \approx 1$ for all delays; offset-charge-shifting events occur at 1.4 h$^{-1}$ and 2.0 h$^{-1}$ for the two detectors respectively, with 6 simultaneous coincidences at 0.43 h$^{-1}$, accounting for 22–57% of large discrete charge steps.

papers.title: Electro-optic conversion of itinerant Fock states
papers.abstract: Superconducting qubits are a leading candidate for utility-scale quantum computing due to their fast gate speeds and steadily decreasing error rates. The requirement for millikelvin operating temperatures, however, creates a significant scaling bottleneck. Modular architectures using optical fiber links could bridge separate cryogenic nodes, but superconducting circuits do not have coherent optical transitions and microwave-to-optical conversion has not been shown for any non-classical photon state. In this work, we demonstrate the on-demand generation and tomographic reconstruction of itinerant single microwave photons at 8.9 GHz from a superconducting qubit. We upconvert this non-Gaussian state with a transducer added noise below 0.012 quanta and count the converted telecom photons at 193.4 THz with a signal-to-noise ratio of up to 5.1$\pm$1.1. We characterize the trade-offs between throughput and noise, and establish a viable path toward heralded entanglement distribution and gate teleportation. Looking ahead, these results empower existing superconducting devices to take a key role in distributed quantum technologies and heterogeneous quantum systems.

summary.summary: This work demonstrates on-demand generation and upconversion of itinerant single microwave photons at 8.9 GHz from a superconducting transmon qubit to telecom-wavelength light at 193.4 THz using an electro-optic transducer based on a lithium niobate whispering gallery mode resonator. The transducer operates at exceptionally low added noise of 0.012 quanta and achieves a signal-to-noise ratio of $5.1 	imes$ the measurement uncertainty, enabling quantum networking with superconducting circuits.
summary.motivation: Superconducting qubits require millikelvin operation due to thermal noise swamping the 10 GHz microwave modes at room temperature, creating a fundamental scaling bottleneck for quantum networks. Bridging microwave and optical domains via coherent transduction of non-classical states is essential for distributed quantum technologies, but microwave-to-optical conversion of itinerant non-Gaussian photon states has not been previously demonstrated.
summary.method: A transmon qubit in a 3D aluminum cavity generates single microwave Fock states via blue sideband driving. The itinerant photons propagate through a coaxial cable to an electro-optic transducer consisting of a superconducting microwave cavity with an embedded 2.5 mm radius LiNbO$_3$ disk resonator with thin-film aluminum electrodes. An optical pump at 193.4 THz upconverts the microwave photons via the Pockels effect, and upconverted photons are filtered through four cascaded Fabry-Perot cavities and detected with a superconducting nanowire single-photon detector.
summary.result: Microwave single-photon Fock states with fidelity 97.6% are generated and tomographically reconstructed. Upconverted optical single photons are detected with $	ext{SNR} = 5.1 	imes 10^{0}$ and input-referred added noise $N_{	ext{add}}^{	ext{up}} = 0.012$ quanta at 1 kHz repetition rate, with quantum channel capacity reaching $2.9$ Hz at 20 kHz repetition rate, placing the transducer squarely in the quantum limit ($N_{	ext{add}}^{	ext{up}} < 1$).

papers.title: Long-range phase coherence and phase patterns in hybrid Josephson junction arrays
papers.abstract: The coherence of superconductivity and its suppression near a quantum phase transition is governed by the interplay between local pairing and macroscopic phase coherence. Using scanning SQUID, we image the local susceptibility in a hybrid Josephson junction array. On a square lattice of narrow islands, we simultaneously access both the amplitude and spatial phase structure of sensitive superconducting states. We observe periodic phase patterns at commensurate magnetic fillings. At zero field the long-range phase coherence is strongest. At a finite field, smaller than one percent of flux quantum per unit cell, the system fragments into large regions of constant superconducting phase, as a function of the applied field. Our results provide the first direct measurement of long-range phase coherence in a Josephson junction array.

summary.summary: This work uses scanning SQUID microscopy to directly image the spatial phase structure and susceptibility of a square-lattice hybrid Josephson junction array, revealing periodic phase patterns at commensurate magnetic fillings and fragmentation into phase-locked domains at fields $< 1\%$ of $\Phi_0$ per unit cell. The measurements provide the first direct observation of long-range superconducting phase coherence in such arrays and its suppression across a quantum phase transition.
summary.motivation: Understanding how macroscopic phase coherence emerges from local pairing and how it breaks down near quantum critical points requires direct access to the spatial phase structure of superconducting states, which has not been experimentally resolved in Josephson junction arrays.
summary.method: The authors fabricated a square lattice of narrow superconducting islands and used scanning SQUID microscopy to simultaneously measure the local susceptibility amplitude and phase in each junction, recording phase patterns as a function of applied magnetic field.
summary.result: At zero field, long-range phase coherence is maximal; at fields exceeding $\sim 0.01 \Phi_0$ per plaquette, the array fragments into macroscopic regions of uniform superconducting phase, with periodic phase structures appearing at rational flux fillings.
